headline: BPCL's profit falls 22.5% to ₹4,993 crore as a five-month freeze on fuel prices eats into strong refining margins
summary: State-run Bharat Petroleum reported July–September standalone net profit of ₹4,993 crore, down from ₹6,443 crore a year earlier, even though revenue from operations rose to ₹1.58 lakh crore from ₹1.22 lakh crore. Its refineries earned a gross refining margin of $32.53 a barrel, three times the $10.78 of a year ago, and ran at 118% of capacity. But Business Standard reported that those gains were wiped out by losses from the five-month-old freeze on retail fuel price revisions while costs kept rising. BPCL also booked a ₹330 crore marketing inventory loss and a ₹397 crore foreign exchange loss. On a consolidated basis, profit fell 21.5% to ₹4,863 crore.
concept_note: When the selling price is held fixed while costs climb, the price can no longer move to where supply and demand would settle it, and the seller absorbs the gap. BPCL's quarter shows the cost of keeping a price away from its market level.
source_name: Business Standard (also reported by Millennium Post)
teaser_title: BPCL's refineries earned three times more per barrel. Its profit still fell 22.5%. Blame a frozen price.
teaser: Revenue jumped to ₹1.58 lakh crore, yet pump prices have not been revised for five months while costs rose. Somebody pays when a price is not allowed to move. The market equilibrium card explains why.

headline: Kotak Mahindra Bank's profit rises 26% to ₹5,645 crore, but costly foreign-currency deposits squeeze its margin
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank reported consolidated net profit of ₹5,645 crore for July–September, up 26% from ₹4,468 crore a year earlier; standalone profit rose 29% to ₹4,212 crore. Net interest income grew 16% to ₹8,459 crore and provisions fell 15% to ₹803 crore. Its net interest margin slipped to 4.31% from 4.53% in the June quarter, which the bank put down largely to about ₹55,344 crore of FCNR(B) deposits raised under the RBI's special window. Gross bad loans improved to 1.04% from 1.39% a year ago, while net advances grew 25% and deposits 23%. The Hindu reported that profit beat estimates compiled by LSEG but fell short of some brokerages' forecasts.
concept_note: The headline profit, the interest income line, the margin and the bad-loan ratio each tell a different part of the story. Reading the statements together shows how profit can rise while the margin on each rupee lent shrinks.
source_name: Business Standard (also reported by The Hindu and The Economic Times)
teaser_title: Kotak raised over ₹55,000 crore of deposits in one quarter. That is largely why its margin shrank.
teaser: Profit rose 26% and bad loans fell, but money gathered through the RBI's special foreign-currency window cost more, pulling the margin down to 4.31%. Profit is only one line of the story. The financial statements card shows how to read the rest.

headline: Houthis claim attacks on Saudi oil sites and airports as Air India suspends Riyadh and Dammam flights until 7 November
summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed on Saturday that they had attacked oil facilities and airports across Saudi Arabia, naming an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh refinery and airports in Riyadh, Dammam and Najran, according to Reuters as cited by Bombay Samachar; Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the claims. Yanbu, on the Red Sea, has become an important alternative export route for Saudi crude while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is disrupted. The same day, Air India and Air India Express said flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam would stay suspended until 7 November and Jeddah services until 31 October, offering free rebooking or full refunds. IndiGo has cancelled its Jeddah, Dammam and Madinah flights until 31 October.
concept_note: Threats to refineries and export terminals raise the risk that less oil reaches the market, which is one of the things that shifts the supply curve. The same conflict is also cutting the supply of air travel between India and Saudi Arabia.
source_name: Bombay Samachar (citing Reuters); also reported by The Tribune (ANI)
teaser_title: The Houthis say they hit Saudi oil sites. Indian flights to Riyadh are now grounded until 7 November.
teaser: Yanbu, which they named as a target, is Saudi Arabia's route around a disrupted Hormuz, and Air India, IndiGo and Akasa have all pulled flights. When supply is at risk, prices follow. The law of supply card shows what shifts the curve.

headline: Sebi reviews short-selling rules and plans AI guidelines with kill switches, while NSE checks its network for AI cyber threats
summary: Sebi chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Saturday that the regulator is reviewing short selling and securities lending and borrowing to improve liquidity and price discovery, and is building safeguards against misuse of trading terminals. Speaking at the ANMI brokers' convention in Mumbai, he said Sebi is finalising guidelines on responsible use of AI that would include clear accountability, data controls, kill switches and human oversight, and is exploring an AI sandbox to test new tools safely. Sebi is also working on a market-making framework for corporate bonds and lighter compliance for smaller brokers. At the same event, NSE chief Ashish Kumar Chauhan said the exchange is reviewing every part of its network for weaknesses as AI-based cyberattacks rise.
concept_note: Kill switches, human oversight and named accountability are governance tools: they make sure someone answers for what an algorithm does. Sebi is applying the logic of corporate governance to AI in trading.
teaser_title: Algorithms now place a growing share of trades. Sebi wants a human, and a kill switch, behind each one.
teaser: The regulator is drafting AI rules, reviewing short selling and planning an AI sandbox, while NSE hunts for weak spots in its network. 'Who is accountable?' is the oldest question in governance. The corporate governance card explains it.

headline: IDFC First Bank's profit nearly triples to ₹1,045 crore as provisions for bad loans fall
summary: IDFC First Bank reported July–September net profit of ₹1,045 crore, up about 197% from a year earlier, helped mainly by lower provisions and better asset quality. Total provisions fell to ₹1,137 crore from ₹1,452 crore, and gross bad loans dropped to ₹4,467 crore from ₹4,841 crore. Net interest income rose 21% to ₹6,184 crore, deposits grew 25.9% and loans 30.1%. The bank raised ₹34,390 crore of FCNR(B) deposits in the quarter, which CEO V. Vaidyanathan said cost about 1% less than comparable domestic deposits once priority-sector benefits are included.
concept_note: A provision is money a lender sets aside for losses it judges probable on loans it has already made. When fewer loans look likely to go bad, provisions shrink and that saving flows straight into profit.
teaser_title: IDFC First's profit nearly tripled, mostly because it had to set aside less money for bad loans.
teaser: Provisions fell by over ₹300 crore and bad loans shrank, turning a modest year into a ₹1,045 crore quarter. What a bank expects to lose shapes what it reports today. The provisions card explains how.

headline: Kolkata households pay more for Lakshmi Puja as idol prices rise ₹100–200 on higher transport costs
summary: With Kojagori Lakshmi Puja on Sunday, Kolkata shoppers are paying more for idols, puja items and bhog vegetables, Millennium Post reported. At Jadubabur Bazar in south Kolkata, Lakshmi idols sell for ₹150 to ₹1,600, and a seller said prices are up about ₹100–200 per idol from last year because transport costs more. At Koley market, beans sell for ₹60–75 a kg, tomatoes ₹35–45 and potatoes ₹30–40, while coconuts cost ₹35–65 each. Some traders said sales were sluggish and profits thin, but buyers said the ritual could not be skipped even at higher prices.
concept_note: When buyers say they will purchase something whatever the price, demand is price-inelastic: a higher price barely reduces how much they buy. That is why sellers can pass rising transport costs on to customers at festival time.
teaser_title: Lakshmi idols cost up to ₹200 more in Kolkata this year. Families are buying them anyway.
teaser: From Jadubabur Bazar to Koley market, transport costs have lifted puja prices, yet buyers say the ritual cannot be skipped. When demand barely falls as prices rise, sellers gain pricing power. The price elasticity card explains why.

headline: China opposes a US plan to widen curbs on American investment in its tech sectors and reserves the right to retaliate
summary: China's commerce ministry on Saturday urged the United States to stop expanding restrictions on American investment in China, calling a new US Treasury proposal discriminatory, Reuters reported via Business Recorder. The proposal, issued on Thursday, would add biotechnology to the restricted sectors and widen coverage of high-performance computing and hypersonic systems; existing rules already limit some US investment in Chinese semiconductors, quantum technology and AI. Beijing said the plan runs against the consensus reached by the two presidents and that it reserves the right to take countermeasures, without giving details. The US Treasury says the rules are not aimed only at China and are meant to stop US money from funding dual-use technologies that could threaten national security.
concept_note: Government rules on where capital may flow are part of the political and legal environment that firms cannot control but must plan around. A PESTLE scan would flag this as a risk for any company with US–China exposure.
source_name: Business Recorder (Reuters); also reported by Xinhua
teaser_title: Washington wants to stop US money funding Chinese biotech and supercomputers. Beijing is threatening to hit back.
teaser: The proposed rules would add biotechnology to a list that already covers chips, quantum and AI. For global firms, a policy line drawn in Washington can redraw a business plan. The marketing environment card explains how to scan for it.

headline: Commerce Ministry is mapping 'AI-proof' professions where India could lead globally, says Piyush Goyal
summary: Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said his ministry has started identifying professions that are less likely to be replaced by artificial intelligence, The Hindu reported. Speaking to Indian researchers and students in Germany on Friday, he said the focus would be on sectors where AI can add efficiency without replacing people, naming handicrafts, handloom, culinary arts and tourism as areas where India could take a global lead. He said support would be a mix of private, government and people-led efforts, and that incentives would not be needed for every activity. Goyal also said attracting Indian researchers back home depends not just on money but on a supportive environment for research.
concept_note: Technology changing which jobs exist, and how people work alongside it, is one of the big challenges organisational behaviour now has to deal with. Planning for 'AI-proof' work is a national version of that problem.
teaser_title: The government is drawing up a list of jobs AI can't take. Handloom and cooking are on Goyal's list.
teaser: The Commerce Ministry wants to know which work AI will only speed up rather than replace, and where India's people give it an edge. Your future job is part of that question. The OB challenges card explains why it matters to managers.

headline: New ethanol tender's prices tilt demand towards rice over maize, worrying grain distillers and sugar mills
summary: Oil marketing companies' ethanol tender for 2026–27 sets procurement prices of ₹60.32 a litre for surplus foodgrains, ₹64 for damaged foodgrains and ₹66 for maize plus ₹2.79, The Hindu reported. Ethanol made from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses has been left out, while C-heavy molasses ethanol remains eligible. The Grain Ethanol Manufacturers Association says the tender puts a disproportionate burden on rice-based feedstock and could weaken maize's role, and it has asked for clarity on how allocations will be split under a lowest-price system. Industry estimates suggest damaged-foodgrain ethanol allocation could top 700 crore litres in 2026–27, against about 60 crore litres the year before. The sugar industry body ISMA welcomed the exclusions but objected to priority given to dedicated ethanol plants with long-term contracts.
concept_note: Rice and maize are substitutes as ethanol feedstock, so the price set for one changes demand for the other. Cross elasticity measures exactly that link between two products.
teaser_title: A few rupees per litre may shift ethanol-making from maize to rice. Grain distillers are alarmed.
teaser: The new tender prices rice-based ethanol below maize and leaves cane juice out, and the industry expects damaged-grain ethanol to jump from about 60 crore to over 700 crore litres. When two inputs can replace each other, one price moves both. The cross elasticity card explains it.

headline: AU Small Finance Bank's profit jumps 53% to ₹858 crore as it prepares to become a universal bank
summary: AU Small Finance Bank, India's largest small finance bank, reported July–September net profit of ₹858 crore, up from ₹561 crore a year earlier, The Economic Times reported. Net interest income rose 32% to ₹2,820 crore and its net interest margin improved to 5.8% from 5.5%. Gross bad loans fell to 1.99% and provisions dropped 25% to ₹359 crore. Its loan book grew 25% to ₹1.54 lakh crore and deposits 29% to ₹1.70 lakh crore. Founded in 1996 as a vehicle financier, AU is in the process of becoming a universal bank.
concept_note: Becoming a universal bank means competing head-on with large established lenders for the same customers and deposits. Porter's Five Forces help judge how intense that rivalry is and what advantage AU must build to win.
source_name: The Economic Times (also reported by Business Standard)
teaser_title: It started in 1996 financing vehicles. Now AU's profit is up 53% and it wants to take on the big banks.
teaser: India's largest small finance bank grew loans 25% and widened its margin as it moves to become a universal lender. Stepping into a bigger league means bigger rivals. The Five Forces card shows how to size up that fight.

headline: Government gives companies until 31 December to file FY26 financial statements without extra fees after portal glitches
summary: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs has extended the deadline for companies to file their 2025–26 financial statements on Form AOC-4, including consolidated and XBRL versions, to 31 December 2026 without additional fees, Business Standard reported. Annual returns on Forms MGT-7 and MGT-7A can now be filed until 31 January 2027. The move follows complaints from company secretaries about the MCA-21 Version 3 portal; the Institute of Company Secretaries of India had cited frequent downtime, logouts and form validation failures. The ministry's 24 October circular does not extend the deadlines for holding annual general meetings.
concept_note: Filed financial statements are how outsiders such as the government registry, investors and lenders see a company's accounts. The deadline matters because these users rely on timely reports.
teaser_title: The company-filing portal kept failing. Now firms have until 31 December to file their accounts free.
teaser: After complaints about downtime and failed forms, the ministry has pushed the free-filing deadline for FY26 financial statements to 31 December. Accounts exist so others can read them. The 'who uses accounting' card explains who is waiting.

headline: JK Cement's profit rises 6% to ₹169 crore on higher volumes, and its paints arm plans a ₹130 crore plant in Telangana
summary: JK Cement reported consolidated net profit of ₹169.3 crore for July–September, up 6.31% from ₹159.25 crore a year earlier, as revenue rose 23.65% to ₹3,733 crore. Grey cement volumes grew 21% to 5.37 million tonnes and white cement 13% to 0.49 million tonnes, though total expenses rose 24%. Its board also approved a new 75,000-kilolitre water-based paint plant in Telangana's Suryapet district for its subsidiary JK Maxx Paints, at an estimated cost of ₹130 crore. The existing Bhiwadi plant runs at 60% utilisation, and the company expects it to be fully used by FY28, which is why it is adding capacity.
concept_note: Building a plant before the current one is full only makes sense if the company is confident about future demand. Estimating that demand correctly decides whether new capacity pays off or sits idle.
teaser_title: JK Cement's paint factory is only 60% busy. It is still building a second one. Here's the bet behind it.
teaser: Cement volumes grew 21%, and the company expects its paints plant to be fully used by FY28, so it is adding a ₹130 crore plant now. Capacity decisions are demand forecasts in concrete. The demand estimation card shows how they are made.
